title: Book 3 — Thalia, Chapter 117
paragraphs: There is a plain in Asia bounded by mountains on every side, and through the mountains there are five clefts. This plain once belonged to the Chorasmians and lies on the borders of the Chorasmians themselves, the Hyrcanians, Parthians, Sarangians, and Thamanaians; but ever since the Persians came to rule, it has belonged to the king. From this encircling mountain range of which I speak flows a great river called the Akes. In former times this river, divided into five streams and conducted through a separate cleft in the mountains to each separate nation, used to water the lands of the peoples just mentioned. But since they have come under the Persians, they have suffered as follows. The king has built up the clefts in the mountains and set gates at each cleft. Now that the water has been cut off from its outlet, the plain within the mountains has become a sea, because the river runs into it and has no outlet anywhere. Those, therefore, who in former times had depended on the water can no longer use it and are in great distress. For during winter they have rain from heaven like everyone else, but in summer they need the water when they sow millet and sesame seed. So when the water is not granted them, they come to the Persians together with their wives, and standing at the gates of the king's court they cry and howl; and the king orders that, for those who need it most, the gates leading to their land be opened. Then when their land has been satisfied with the water, these gates are closed again, and he orders the gates to be opened for others—namely, whichever of the rest has the greatest need. As I have heard, he exacts large sums of money for opening them, on top of the regular tribute.
